Probably, but there's also a chance that Microsoft working closely with FOSS projects will have a perverse negative effect on said projects. For example, look at the "embrace, extend, extinguish" strategy. If Microsoft offers a lot of products that are compatible with open-source offerings, but only actually makes token contributions to the community, they see the benefit of interoperability - customers are happy, and can easily switch between the two products - while also starving the open-source project of development effort. At that point, they can make incremental changes to add value but leave the actual open-source projects rushing to catch up, giving the open-source alternative an undeserved reputation as "always two steps behind." At that point, it's not much effort for an open-source-user to become a formerly-open-source-user because, remember, the first step in the process was to make the two work together well.

You're absolutely right, of course. One of the most frustrating things about being a Linux user and not a Linux developer is that disconnect between the user's goals and the developer's goals. That leaves a lot of potential users in the cold, so to speak, because developers want to spend their time developing software, not supporting it.

The way I see it, there are two major ways to defend against this problematic strategy: First, we make sure our projects don't waste time "keeping up with Microsoft". It'll take backbone, and not a little bit of PR, but if Microsoft's added features are seen as nonstandard behavior rather than improvements, the burden of justifying and supporting their changes is on them, not us.

Secondly, we really need more monetary support for user support. Everybody knows you still have to pay the bills, so even if somebody wants to spend their time improving the Linux user experience, they can't do it without money. The few times we've seen this really take off(Red Hat, Canonical, etc.), the people doing the hard work are still being motivated by profit from selling their products to the users. That's not a bad thing to do, to be sure, but it still means they're susceptible to losing their market share. I've been dying to see a patronage system of software development for years, and thank god, it's finally here in the form of Patreon et al. We as a community really need to be pushing that. Donate to your friendly neighborhood developers and maintainers, not to earn the right to use their software, but to ensure they have a future in continuing to make it!
